note_tweet.text:
SpaceX has officially announced that it is currently targeting November 13th at 5:45 PM ET for Starship's 15th flight.

Flight info: 
"This flight is planned to be the first to return both Starship and Super Heavy to the launch site for catch. If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket."

• Flight will last more than 22 hours, completing approximately 14 orbits around Earth.
• Starship will orbit at an altitude of approximately 275 km (171 miles).
• First attempt to recover both Super Heavy and Starship at the launch site during the same mission.
• First return-to-launch-site and catch attempt for a Super Heavy V3 booster.
• Super Heavy will execute launch, ascent, stage separation, boostback burn, and return to Starbase for a tower catch.
• Starship will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites into orbit before attempting its first return to Starbase and tower catch.
• The 26 satellites will provide capacity equivalent to approximately 10 Falcon 9 launches carrying Starlink V2 Mini satellites.
• Satellites will deploy antennas and solar arrays, establish radio and laser communications, and raise their orbits using onboard thrusters.
• Satellites could begin serving customers within weeks of launch following successful on-orbit checkouts.
• Three Starlink V3 satellites will carry cameras to inspect Starship's heatshield and transmit imagery to ground operators.
• Starship's heatshield will feature improved tile retention, additional protection against plasma intrusion, and expanded use of curved tiles to reduce heating between tiles.
• Starship will only attempt its return and catch if critical reentry, landing burn, and tower approach systems are confirmed healthy.
• Multiple predetermined ocean deorbit locations and a passively safe suborbital trajectory provide contingency options.
• A successful mission would mark the first complete recovery of an orbital launch system, a major milestone toward rapid reusability.

More info: https://t.co/PxrUMYLkOv

note_tweet.text:
In 2004, before SpaceX had launched a single rocket, Elon Musk told CNN that what his company was doing was critical to the future of NASA.

He was 33, two years into SpaceX, sitting down with CNN in California in July 2004. He said cheaper launches were the way to help NASA, that supplying bases on the Moon and Mars would be a huge business, and that SpaceX would start with uncrewed flights and then carry people.

"What I think we're beginning to see is the dawn of a new era of space exploration."
SpaceX's first rocket reached orbit in 2008. In 2020, SpaceX became the first private company to fly NASA astronauts to the space station. In 2021, NASA picked Starship to land its astronauts on the Moon.
Video: CNN @elonmusk

note_tweet.text:
NASA is betting BIG on SpaceX for the future of lunar exploration, expanding its role across THREE major areas of Moon Base infrastructure: lunar cargo delivery, space transportation, and communications

And Starship has been selected for a major new mission in 2028 to deploy communications satellites around the Moon

Here's how SpaceX is becoming a major part of NASA's Moon Base ambitions:

1. LUNAR CARGO DELIVERY

NASA has selected SpaceX as one of eight companies under its new CLPS 2 framework, a 10-year program worth up to $10 BILLION across all providers

This positions SpaceX to compete for future missions delivering critical science equipment, technology, and infrastructure directly to the lunar surface

2. SPACE TRANSPORTATION

SpaceX's Falcon 9 is among the launch vehicles named for NASA's newly awarded lunar transportation missions

Falcon 9's proven launch capabilities will support missions involving spacecraft transportation, navigation testing, and infrastructure needed for NASA's expanding lunar operations

3. LUNAR COMMUNICATIONS

NASA has directly selected SpaceX for a major Starship mission in 2028

Starship will deploy communications satellites into cislunar space, helping establish the communications infrastructure needed to support astronauts, spacecraft, and future operations around the Moon

This is MUCH bigger than simply landing astronauts on the lunar surface

NASA is building toward a sustained human presence on the Moon, and that requires an entire transportation and infrastructure network

From launching spacecraft with Falcon 9 to competing for lunar cargo deliveries and deploying communications infrastructure with Starship, SpaceX is positioning itself across all THREE critical areas

And Starship is becoming an important part of NASA's plans for humanity's permanent presence beyond Earth
